sections.h2: Where Hays County keeps its records
sections.html:
The Hays County Clerk's Records Division is the county's keeper of official public records, an archive that runs back to 1848. It holds deeds, deeds of trust and liens. Search and buy copies through the clerk's online Self-Service portal, use the computers in the office lobby, or ask to read an archived record book at the counter. Questions about official records can go to recordsdivision@hayscountytx.gov.

Three divisions make up the clerk's office: Records, Courts and Commissioners Court. Courts handles probate and guardianship support, so start there if the homeowner has died. The District Clerk, a different office, holds divorce and family court files, and a decree that touches your title may mean a second stop.

San Marcos is the main location. Three substations also serve the public. All keep weekday hours of 8 am to 4:30 pm with a noon to 1 pm lunch break. Phone first to learn whether a substation will take your filing.

The Self-Service portal opens with a disclaimer you must accept before you search. The clerk makes no certification of what the index displays, treats it as a rough catalogue, and urges you to try each spelling a name might take. Use the index to find the recorded document, then open the document itself and read it.

Four searches, run before listing, catch most nasty surprises:

  • Each owner on the chain of title, searched with and without middle initials, suffixes and former surnames.
  • Every deed of trust, followed by its matching release. A loan paid off years back can still look open when nobody filed the release.
  • Judgments, abstracts and state tax liens, which the Comptroller reports to the county clerk for entry in a separate lien book.
  • Notices of foreclosure sale, which the clerk posts and files.

A free service called Fraud Guard emails you whenever a document bearing your name is recorded. For a rental house or vacant lot, that is an inexpensive early warning against a forged deed.

Texas law (Property Code 12.001(b)) bars a clerk from recording a deed until the signature has been acknowledged to a notary or similar officer, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses. Venue follows the parcel: whether the house is in Kyle, Wimberley or Dripping Springs, and wherever the seller now lives, the deed goes to Hays County.

Besides ordinary warranty deeds, the deed records take quitclaims, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, affidavits, lien releases, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney. The fee stacks up: $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for every page after, and then county add-ons for records management, archives and technology. If the grantee's mailing address is absent, expect $25 more. Request the exact total from the clerk prior to mailing.

Some buyers in federal or state grant programs can have recording fees waived if the commissioners court so directs its clerk. When your buyer is in such a program, ask whether Hays County has adopted a waiver.

sections.h2: Hays County housing at a glance
sections.html: Hays County has grown fast since 2020. The mid-2025 estimate is 304,390 residents, a rise of 26.3% from the 2020 base, with 120,266 housing units. About 64.1% of homes are owner-occupied, and the middle value of those homes is $399,800. New subdivisions mean new plats, deeds of trust and liens, so a recently built house often carries more recorded paper than one that changed hands twice in thirty years.

sections.h2: Who values property and sends the tax bill?
sections.html:
Money matters belong to two other offices, not the clerk. Values, the property search and exemptions come from the Hays Central Appraisal District in Kyle. Bills and payments come from the Hays County Tax Office, because the district neither mails bills nor collects.

The district's office is 21001 North IH 35 in Kyle, phone (512) 268-2522, with a front-door drop box and weekday hours of 8 to 5. Its online forms cover a homestead exemption, an agricultural use application, a business personal property rendition and a change of address. Bills and payment instructions are at tax.co.hays.tx.us.

Each granted homestead gets an audit every five years (Tax Code 11.43(h-1)). Answer an audit letter promptly, enclosing a valid Texas driver's license or state ID with the house address on it, because silence puts a termination date on the exemption. Statewide, values are fixed January 1; homestead notices begin about April 1; protests are generally due by mid-May.

sections.h2: Record problems that slow a Hays County sale
sections.html:
Stale liens, tax arrears and absent heirs head the list. On January 1 each year a lien secures that year's tax, so whatever is unpaid stays attached through a sale. February 1 turns a bill still open after January 31 delinquent, adding a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest.

Inherited houses raise their own questions:

  • A transfer on death deed works only if recorded during the owner's life.
  • For a muniment of title, the court order and will go on file with the clerk.
  • An affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement filed with the clerk, though a buyer or title company has no legal duty to rely on it.
  • Heirs whose names are not on a recorded deed must hand the appraisal district three things before claiming the homestead exemption: an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a current utility bill.

Foreclosure notices reach the clerk at least 21 days ahead of the first-Tuesday auction. Seeing one against a house means a countdown has begun.

Start by downloading the chain of title and noting each owner's name exactly as written. Pair every deed of trust with its release. Get a balance from the Hays County Tax Office for this year and earlier ones. Make sure the appraisal district has your homestead exemption and a correct mailing address. Where the owner has died, work out with a title company which route moves title to the buyer: probate, muniment of title or affidavit of heirship.

An as-is cash buyer still wants a clean transfer, so the title company records the new deed and any payoff releases with the clerk. Closing a gap in the records early protects the closing date.

On closing day, the title company pays off recorded loans, collects the tax due and sends the new deed to the clerk. Ask it for a list of what it found in the records so no item catches you by surprise at the table.

faqs.q: Which office records a deed in Hays County?
faqs.a: The Records Division of the Hays County Clerk handles it, and its files reach back to 1848. A Hays County house is always filed with the Hays County Clerk.

faqs.q: Can I search Hays County deeds online?
faqs.a: Yes, through the clerk's Self-Service portal, where records can be viewed and purchased. You accept a disclaimer first, and the portal advises trying every spelling of a name.

faqs.q: Does the appraisal district record my deed?
faqs.a: No. The appraisal district sets value and handles exemptions from Kyle, while the clerk records the deed. Owners usually update the district separately, for example with its online change of address form.

faqs.q: Who sends the Hays County property tax bill?
faqs.a: The Hays County Tax Office mails the bills and accepts payment. Call it, not the appraisal district, with any question about an amount owed.

faqs.q: What happens if a deed has no grantee mailing address?
faqs.a: The clerk may add a $25 charge. List a mailing address for every buyer on the deed before you file.
